title: Fiber classes: Aβ, Aδ, C
objective: Classify sensory fibers by diameter, myelination and conduction speed, and link each class to a sensation.

steps.title: Three main cables
steps.body:
Sensory axons sort into three classes by size and [[myelination|myelin]]:

- **Aβ:** large, myelinated, fast. Mostly gentle touch and vibration.
- **Aδ:** thin, lightly myelinated, medium speed. Sharp 'first' pain and cool.
- **C:** unmyelinated, slow. Burning 'second' pain, warmth, itch, and most visceral sensation.

Bigger and myelinated means faster (A2-L4).

visual.alt: Three sensory axons stacked: a thick heavily myelinated Aβ fiber, a thin lightly myelinated Aδ fiber, and an unmyelinated C fiber. The same signal reaches the far end first on Aβ, then Aδ, and last on C.
visual.caption: Same stimulus, three speeds: Aβ fastest, C slowest.

steps.prompt: Match each fiber class to a typical role.
pairs: Slow, burning 'second' pain and most visceral signals
steps.explanation: Stub your toe and you feel the sharp Aδ pain first, then the slower C-fiber ache, a direct readout of conduction speed.

steps.prompt: Why do most visceral (gut, pancreas) sensations travel in slow C fibers?
options: By a strict rule, the viscera are permitted to have only C fibers
Visceral afferents are mostly thin, unmyelinated C fibers, hence slow
Because C fibers are in fact the fastest-conducting class of axon
Because the brain simply ignores the Aβ input from the viscera
steps.explanation: Visceral innervation is dominated by thin fibers. That matches the vague, slow quality of gut sensation (A1-L3).

variants.setup: Most gut and pancreas sensation arrives slowly.
variants.prompt: Which fiber type best fits that?
options: They are thick, myelinated Aβ fibers
They are mostly thin, unmyelinated C fibers
They are the fastest axons in the body
They carry no sensory signal at all
variants.reveal: Slow, vague visceral sensation fits thin, unmyelinated C fibers — the dominant visceral afferent class.

steps.setup: You record conduction velocity to classify an afferent, and get a fast, myelinated response.
steps.prompt: Before calling it 'touch,' what else should you check?
options: Nothing further; conduction speed alone is enough to call it touch
What stimuli actually drive it, since speed and modality are separate
The color of the dye used to fill and label the recorded fiber
Only the temperature of the room during the recording session
steps.reveal: Conduction class and what a neuron responds to are related but not identical. The colon paper measured both speed and force threshold for each subtype, rather than assuming one from the other.

variants.prompt: You record a fast, myelinated afferent. Before labeling it a 'touch' fiber, you should check…
options: Which dye color was used to fill it
What stimuli actually drive it, since speed isn't modality
How old the recorded mouse was
Only the temperature of the room
variants.explanation: Conduction class and modality are separate axes; some fast fibers are high-threshold. The colon paper measured both for each subtype.
